wstep: This card describes the NCHFP recipe for fermented dill pickles, in which the brine contains vinegar.

akapity: For each gallon of container capacity, NCHFP lists 4 pounds of 4-inch pickling cucumbers, 1/2 cup of salt, 1/4 cup of 5% vinegar and 8 cups of water.
Garlic and dried red pepper are optional.
Cut off and discard a 1/16-inch slice from the blossom end, because it may contain softening enzymes.
Do not reduce the amount of salt.
Throughout fermentation the cucumbers must stay 1–2 inches (about 2.5–5 cm) under the brine.
At 70–75 °F (21–24 °C) fermentation takes about 3–4 weeks.
At 55–65 °F (13–18 °C) it also works, but takes 5–6 weeks.
Avoid temperatures above 80 °F (27 °C), or the pickles will become soft.
Check the container several times a week and promptly remove surface scum or mold.
Fully fermented pickles may be kept in the original container in the refrigerator for about 4–6 months, if surface scum and mold are removed regularly.
NCHFP calls canning a better way to store them.
To can them, pour the brine into a pan, heat it slowly to a boil and simmer for 5 minutes.
Fill the jars with the pickles and hot brine, leaving 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) of headspace.
Water-bath canning, raw pack, at 0–1000 ft (up to 300 m) above sea level takes 10 minutes for pint jars and 15 minutes for quart jars.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.
At 1001–6000 ft (above 300 m up to 1800 m) process pints for 15 minutes and quarts for 20.
Above 6000 ft (above 1800 m) process pints for 20 minutes and quarts for 25.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m, 3000 ft becomes 900 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
NCHFP times are for US jar sizes: a pint holds about 473 ml and a quart about 946 ml.
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): for a jar of up to 473 ml use the pint time, and for a larger jar of up to 946 ml, for example 0.5 l or 0.9 l, use the quart time.
This NCHFP recipe gives no time for jars larger than a quart, such as 1 l, so use smaller jars.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.
If the pickles become soft, slimy or develop a disagreeable odor, discard them.
